utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Today is Tuesday, February 5, 2008. Good morning to the Prosecution, to the Defence, and to the accused, and to everyone assisting us in and out of this courtroom. I'm now going to give the floor to Mr. Stringer, who will complete the 98 bis proceedings as far as the Prosecution is concerned. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry while we're waiting, Mr. Stringer, would you mind moving your desk where Mr. Scott's was yesterday. Otherwise, I will be a biased physically so that I can see you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. We're going to -- before I begin I can inform the Trial Chamber that we have loaded a number of the exhibits into the Sanction software programme in order to get a number of them on the screens for the benefit of the counsel and the Judges. So I was a bit closer to Ms. Winner because we're going to be managing this together, but I'm sure we will manage. And may it please the Court, Mr. President and Your Honours, Counsel, good morning to you all. One brief correction. I'll be making the submissions with respect to the accused Mr. Pusic. However, the Trial Chamber will be hearing from Mr. Scott again after I have completed in respect of Valentin Coric, and I think a very brief remark regarding the Petkovic submissions. Mr. President, Your Honours, the Prosecution submits that certainly for purposes of this Rule 98 bis proceeding, the evidence conclusively demonstrates that the accused Berislav Pusic bears criminal possibility with all of the crimes with which he's charged in the indictment. Mr. Pusic's culpability is not only based on the fact that he held several positions of leadership and responsibility within the HVO structures established to arrest, detain, and expel Bosnian Muslim population. The evidence shows that Berislav Pusic in fact exercised his authority and his substantial influence to support the unlawful detention and mistreatment of prisoners. He used his offices and positions of authority as well to bring about the expulsion and deportation of prisoners and their families from their homes throughout the territory of the self-proclaimed Croatian Community or Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. In their Rule 98 bis submissions, the Pusic Defence asserted that the Prosecution had failed to present sufficient evidence as to all counts charging Mr. Pusic, although counsel only specifically addressed some of these counts. Apart from a general denial, counsel did not assert that for any specific count the crime alleged did not actually occur. Mr. President, I do not intend to address the crime base for each of the 26 counts with which Mr. Pusic is charged beyond saying that the Prosecution submits that it has presented ample evidence to establish that the crimes as charged in the indictment were committed. Counsel for Mr. Pusic did challenge the evidence as it relates to the criminal liability of Mr. Pusic for all counts in the indictment, specifically raising different modes of liability under Article 7(1) of the Statute, including joint criminal enterprise, and Article 7(3). For purposes of this Rule 98 bis proceeding, the Trial Chamber need only consider whether the evidence is capable of proving Mr. Pusic's responsibility for each of the crimes he's charged with under any alleged mode of liability. We could talk about Mr. Pusic's responsibility for planning, instigating, ordering, committing, and aiding and abetting a variety of crimes that are charged in the indictment, particularly those crimes that fell directly within the scope of his competence and position. Several of the documents that we will refer to in these submissions establish Mr. Pusic's personal involvement and responsibility for numerous crimes. For purposes of Article 7(3), we could talk about the extent of his effective command and control over HVO personnel, at the very least, those HVO personnel who had custody and control of Bosnian Muslim prisoners and other expelled Muslims, for it is clear that Pusic did, in fact, possess and exercise effective command and control over HVO military units and personnel that had Muslim prisoners and displaced persons in their custody. The documents we review this morning will establish that as well. For this hearing, Mr. President, and to address the points raised by counsel for Mr. Pusic in his submissions last week, we believe that it would be most useful and efficient to talk about Mr. Pusic's criminal responsibility as a member of the joint criminal enterprise that is alleged in the indictment and what the Prosecution regards as his very tangible and substantial contribution to it. To consider Mr. Pusic's role and contribution to the joint criminal enterprise, the Trial Chamber should recall the evidence showing his de jure and de facto authority, as well as his own actions and words. De jure authority. As an officer of the HVO military police, as head of the service for the exchange of prisoners and other persons, and as head of the commission to take charge of all Herceg-Bosna HVO prisons and detention facilities holding POWs and other detainees, Berislav Pusic was responsible for and had significant authority regarding, one, prisoner exchanges involving both civilian detainees and prisoners of war. Two, the release of prisoners who were held at various HVO detention facilities. Three, overseeing HVO prisons and detention camps, record-keeping in those prisons and camps, and conditions of life for the prisoners in the HVO prisons and camps. Four, issuance of the papers that enabled Muslims to flee the Mostar region. Five, and the ultimate transfer or deportation of prisoners and their families to third countries or to territory outside the HVO-held areas in the HZ HB. With the full range of authority he possessed in respect of all prisoners, civilian and combatant, Berislav Pusic determined who was detained, who was released, who was exchanged, and who was evacuated. He implemented HVO policy in these spheres on behalf of his superiors Mate Boban, Jadranko Prlic, Bruno Stojic, and Valentin Coric. Pusic frequently decided where, which prison or camp, prisoners were to be held, at times directing traffic, if you will, ordering the transfer of prisoners from one facility to another in order to create space for more prisoners to come. For prisoners whom he released he decided where they were to be released to or ensure that they were leaving Herceg-Bosna altogether. Pusic gathered detailed data and lists of prisoners. He knew their conditions of confinement. For Bosnian Muslims fortunate enough not to have been arrested but yet unfortunate enough to find themselves living in the new order of a Croat-dominated HZ HB in West Mostar, Pusic facilitated their movement out of Herceg-Bosna through the issuance of transit visas and other papers. These enabled Bosnian Muslims to move through HVO check-points to the Republic of Croatia and on to third countries. That long one-way journey began with the signature of Berislav Pusic. In this way, Pusic played a substantial role in controlling and directing the movement and treatment of Bosnian Muslims in, around, and ultimately out of the territory of the HZ HB or the areas controlled by the HVO. This was Berislav Pusic's contribution to the joint criminal enterprise which had as its goal the permanent removal and ethnic cleansing of Bosnian Muslims and non-Croats from the territory of the HZ HB. In 1992, Berislav Pusic was an officer of the HVO military police in Mostar. On the 2nd of November, 1992, shortly after the events that occurred in Prozor that year, Pusic participated in a meeting with the head of the HVO military police administration, Mr. Coric. Pusic was an officer within the crime prevention department of the 3rd Battalion of the military police based in Mostar. And that is according to Exhibit number P 00696, page 6. In early April of 1993, shortly before the HVO's mid-April offensives in Central Bosnia and Sovici, Doljani, Mr. Pusic was proposed by his superiors in the 3rd Military Police Battalion to serve as a control officer in the military police or as an officer for cooperation and contact with the opposite side regarding exchanges of prisoners. That's Exhibit P 01773. And the next exhibit that we'd like to put up on the screen, Mr. President, is Exhibit P 02020. Mr. President, this is a document dated the 22nd of April, 1993. Three weeks later, on the 22nd of April, 1993, after the sides had signed cease-fire agreements following the HVO's mid-April offensives in Central Bosnia and the HVO attack on Sovici, Doljani in the Jablanica municipality, Valentin Coric accepted the nomination of Pusic and appointed him to participate on behalf of the HVO military police in the exchange of all arrested persons. From this point in April 1993 through to the end of the conflict between the Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Muslims, Berislav Pusic exercised primary responsibility for the exchanges of HVO prisoners. On the 11th of May, 1993, two days after the HVO attack on the ABiH Vranica building, Bruno Stojic, the head of the HVO defence department, specifically appointed Pusic to be HVO liaison officer to the UNPROFOR Spanish Battalion in connection with an exchange in East Mostar. Pusic had negotiated the removal of a priest from East Mostar in exchange for some blood plasma delivered to the east side hospital. That's Exhibit P 02291.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please stop. Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I really do not wish to interrupt my colleague in his presentation. However, I think he is leading the Trial Chamber astray now. This document, P 02291, the translation was corrected with the intervention of the Defence team, and we can see that Mr. Pusic was not in fact appointed liaison officer. I know that Mr. Stringer came into this case a little later, but there was a comment from the -- an objection from the Defence counsel, and the translation was indeed corrected and it's now on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm working with the version that's on e-court, Mr. President, but the document will speak for itself. We would then put on the screen Exhibit P 03191, Mr. President. As the conflict between the HVO and the ABiH intensified, Pusic's powers expanded. On the 5th of July, 1993, five days after the ABiH attack on the HVO northern barracks, Jadranko Prlic, as president of the HVO, signed a decision establishing the service for the exchange of prisoners and other persons. On that same day, in a separate decision, Prlic appointed Berislav Pusic to serve as the head of that service. Pusic's appointment was published in the official HZ HB gazette, the Narodni List, which is in evidence as Exhibit P 03208. Under Article 4 of this decision, on page 2, it was the HVO of the HZ HB that had the authority to appoint and relieve Pusic as the head of the service. The next exhibit is P 03075. Mr. President, at the time of his appointment by Mr. Prlic on the 5th of July, 1993, there was certainly no shortage of prisoners at the disposal of Mr. Pusic for exchange purposes. In the five days following the ABiH attack on the northern barracks, the HVO and its military police units had rounded up hundreds, perhaps thousands, of "persons of Muslim faith" as they are referred to in Exhibit P 03075. This is a document that Mr. Scott referred to yesterday, Mr. President, in his submissions regarding the series of orders that went down the chain of command on the arrest of Muslim -- Muslims of military age in the wake of the ABiH attack on 30 June. According to this document, which is a report of the Capljina military police dated the 1st of July, 1993, one Military Police Platoon was engaged in collecting persons of Muslim faith in Stolac. On page 2, that same report states that: "So far about 1300 persons have been apprehended and brought in from the municipalities of Stolac, Capljina, Mostar and Neum on 30 June and 1 July 1993." These persons of Muslim faith would become Pusic's currency to use in exchanges as a way to facilitate the removal of Muslims from such areas as Capljina, Stolac, and Mostar. It was only their status as Muslims that made them eligible for selection by Pusic to be sent away in an exchange. The next document is P 03052. Mr. President, this exhibit is a document written by Mr. Pusic proposing how the service to which he'd been appointed by Dr. Prlic was to be organised, and it describes his understanding of its responsibilities. The document is undated but it refers specifically to the decision of Jadranko Prlic establishing the office for exchange. According to Mr. Pusic in this document, the responsibilities of his office were "exchanging HVO members as well as civilians, making lists of persons we seek in municipalities, units, and at the level of the HVO operations zones as well as the persons we have exchanged or can exchange, establishing lists ever persons who voluntarily want to leave the areas of the HZ HB, and creating a unified data at the level of the HZ HB ..." using the existing and new information from various sources, including the military police administration. As the HVO continued its massive campaign of arresting Muslims in Western Herzegovina during July of 1993, by early August it found itself in custody of thousands of Muslim prisoners. Exhibit P 09500 is under seal. We're not going to put it up, but it indicates that at a high-level meeting Mr. Boban, on the 21st of July, 1993, stated that some 6.000 Muslims of military age were in custody by that time. We will put up Exhibit P 03995. In an attempt to gain control over the illegal prison system that the HVO leadership had created, and in the face of increasing pressure and criticism from the international community and the Republic of Croatia conditions in these camps, Bruno Stojic appointed Pusic to be the president of commission "authorised by the department of defence to take charge of all detention units and prisons in which POWs and military detainees are held." This occurred on the 6th of August, 1993, this appointment by Mr. Stojic. Of course the term "military detainees" has no real meaning, certainly not in international humanitarian law. This was a code word for civilians who were in HVO prisons and camps only because they were Muslims. The Stojic commission was to be composed of five members with Pusic, who was still acting under the appointment of Dr. Prlic, as head of the service for exchange. Now also as president of the Stojic commission. On page 2 of this document, we see that Stojic ordered that this commission would compile a list of all detainees, sort them into categories, establish control over all detention units and prisons, solve the problems relating to functioning and security, regulate release, regulate prisoner exchanges and the like and any other questions relating to the work and functioning of detention units and prisons. Further, Stojic's order directed that: "The detention unit and prison wardens or commanders must carry out the commands, instructions, and orders and work in accordance with rules prescribed by the commission."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Stringer kindly slow down for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This order of Bruno Stojic gave Pusic an official position of control over the prisoners and the HVO personnel who held them. The next exhibit is 4141. After his appointment as president of the Stojic commission, Berislav Pusic issued a decision exercising his authority as the president of that commission. He required that all detainees be -- that for all detainees a personal data slip be made. On page 2 of the document. He ordered the suspension of all prisoner releases from the Dretelj and Gabela prisons in order to obtain more expeditious registrations and correct classification of prisoners. This decision provided that Berislav Pusic himself, as president of the Stojic commission, would sign off on the final paperwork authorising prisoner releases. Down toward the bottom of what's on the screen, Mr. President, there's a reference here to persons with all guarantees, persons with -- wanting to be released who have the guarantees. The Trial Chamber may recall that the guarantees referred to in this decision relate to guarantees showing that the prisoner would be leaving to go to a third country, and I'll be talking about that more later in my submissions. In his submissions, counsel for Mr. Pusic suggested that Pusic was not a leader or did not play a leadership role in the joint criminal enterprise. The Prosecution disagrees. Mr. President, the evidence discussed thus far clearly demonstrates that the official appointments Berislav Pusic received from Valentin Coric, Bruno Stojic and Jadranko Prlic vested him with substantial de jure powers and authority over Bosnian Muslim prisoners and indeed any Bosnian Muslim in HVO territory who might be useful for exchange purposes. He was also clearly vested with authority over HVO personnel who had Bosnian Muslims in their custody. Was Berislav Pusic subordinate to Messrs. Coric, Stojic, and Prlic? Yes, he was. Witness DZ testified specifically that he believed Pusic was acting in the field on behalf of Messrs. Boban, Prlic, and Stojic and doing their will. That's at page 26513 of the transcript. But this does not mean that Mr. Pusic himself possess a position of leadership and authority regarding the prisons, prisoners, and Bosnian Muslims who sought to flee the persecution and terror directed against them by the HVO. De facto authority. Mr. President, the Prosecution submits that Mr. Pusic's de jure powers as described above translated directly into real, effective, de facto powers on the ground in respect of prisoners and prisoner issues. This should come as no surprise given the fact that his authority emanated directly from personal appointments by the highest authorities in the HVO leadership. Pusic routinely exercised his authority over prisoners and Muslims who sought to leave Herceg-Bosna. He knew and approved of the crimes being directed against Muslim prisoners such as forced labour. On the ground, the evidence establishes that Berislav Pusic was the primary contact person for international representatives wishing to discuss prisoner issues. Pusic was seen by the internationals to be Coric's assistant or right-hand man regarding access to the HVO detention camps at the Heliodrom, Ljubuski, and Capljina. Exhibit 2601 is a letter to Mr. Coric from a representative of the ICRC referring to his 29 May 1993 meeting with Pusic, describing Pusic as Coric's assistant. In their report of 16 June 1993, ECMM monitors Jesus Amatrian and Anton Van der Grinten noted their meeting that day with Mr. Stojic, Coric and Pusic. They wrote that Coric was chief of the HVO military police and Pusic was "deputy HVO military police." That's Exhibit P 02806. The witnesses all testified that Pusic had substantial authority in respect of prisoners and movements of people in and out of HVO territory. Klaus Nisen testified that Pusic was the one to turn to for issues relating to displaced persons, POWs, and sometimes refugees. That's page 20475 of the transcript. Witness BD testified that Pusic was "very clearly powerful," and "had a great deal of influence." Transcript page 20799. Witness BC testified that Pusic's office was responsible for the issuance of all documents that allowed for movement, transit through the territory held by the Bosnian Croats. That's transcript page 18531. Mr. President, could we briefly move into closed session -- or private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Registrar, please, private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Suad Cupina with whom Pusic negotiated in respect of prisoner exchange testified that "We did know, we did know, however, that Berto was the be-all and the end-all for prisoners in the territory of Mostar. He was the one who captured, who released people. So if one wanted someone liberated, released, you had to go and talk to Berto Pusic." Page 4837 to 4838 of the transcript. Mr. President, the evidence shows that Berislav Pusic had substantial de facto, on-the-ground authority matching the de jure authority you would expect of someone appointed to his various positions by Messrs. Coric, Stojic, and Prlic. The evidence shows that Berislav Pusic was directly involved in and had knowledge of virtually every aspect of the situation involving prisoners, conditions of their detention, use of prisoners for forced labour, and release of prisoners to third countries. On the conditions of detention, Pusic personally knew and was regularly informed about the dire and unlawful conditions in which the prisoners were detained. He was repeatedly put on notice of the inadequacy of the facilities, malnutrition, abuse, and mistreatment of the prisoners over whom he had authority. For example, on the 5th of July, 1993, the date of his appointment by Dr. Prlic to head the service for exchange, a report made by the Heliodrom prison warden Stanko Bozic reported an incident in which shooting was directed against the halls in the school at the Heliodrom where prisoners were being held. Bozic noted that the buildings where prisoners were being held had not been built as prisons, so that it was difficult to provide security and protect the detainees in the case of such incidents. He said that the 16 military police officers assigned to secure these buildings were not sufficient. This report was directed to Mr. Coric and Pusic. We can put up Exhibit 5077. This is actually the original language version, Mr. President. That is list of detained persons in the Heliodrom who were being kept in solitary confinement. It's a list of 29 names. It appears over the name and signature of Mr. Pusic. The Trial Chamber has heard testimony in this trial from the first person listed on this document, Ibrahim Saric. The next exhibit is 3334. The warden of the Heliodrom directed reports to Pusic and Coric about suicide attempts in the Heliodrom in July and August of 1993. One of these relates to a suicide attempt by a 65-year-old Muslim prisoner on the 9th of July, 1993. Witness E testified that he would make lists of the prisoners in Ljubuski and that at times Pusic himself would come to Ljubuski prison to get those lists. That's at page 22045 of the transcript. Pusic was present in the Ljubuski facility and knew of the conditions there. Pusic received reports on the sanitary situation at the Gabela and Heliodrom, what were called "preventive isolation centres." That would be Exhibits P 05485 for Gabela and Exhibit P 05503 for the Heliodrom. These reports describe overcrowding and failure to segregate the wounded, sick, and healthy into different wards. Gabela report notes that although the detainees received two meals per day, those engaged in compulsory work got more food. The Trial Chamber will recall the testimony of Ed Vulliamy, who testified that at a press conference about the HVO prison camps Pusic claimed that Dretelj did in fact meet international standards and that regarding those tunnels at Dretelj, which I'm sure the Trial Chamber will recall: "If the tunnels were good enough for the Yugoslav People's Army soldiers, it was good enough for the Muslim prisoners." That's at page 1595 of the transcript, Mr. Vulliamy's testimony. Of course the evidence establishes that the prisoners Pusic was referring to were not just soldiers but also Muslim civilians arrested and detained for preventive isolation. The fact is, Mr. President, that Mr. Pusic had no regard for the treatment of the prisoners in the camps, whether POW or civilian. Access. Not only was Pusic fully informed of the conditions in the camps, he had the authority to grant access into the camps. Philip Watkins testified that they had to get Pusic's approval to gain access to detention facilities. He testified this was a constant battle. Page 18820 of the transcript. Witness BB testified that it was Pusic who granted access to the Heliodrom facility in mid-May 1993 to visit Muslims rounded up and detained there during 9 and 10 May 1993. That's page 17169 and 17239 of the transcript. Forced labour. Mr. President, Berislav Pusic had the power to authorise the use of prisoners for forced labour, and he exercised this power frequently. Josip Praljak who was the deputy warden of the Heliodrom prison facility testified that Pusic exercised this power as a member of the military police. That's page 1470 -- actually, it may be 14741 of the transcript. I will double-check that reference. The next exhibit for the screen is Exhibit P 06805. Mr. President, this is an interesting document in a number of respects. It's a report dated the 22nd of November, 1993, by Radoslav Lavric, who at that time was the newly appointed chief of the military police administration. Coric was at this time the newly appointed minister of interior for the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. This report notes that Pusic could authorise the use of prisoners for work. At the beginning of this report, Lavric states that Pusic is the most competent person to answer questions about the prisoners of war. I also note for Your Honours that in paragraph 2, Lavric writes that it was Valentin Coric who had actually chosen the Heliodrom location as a military prison. The next exhibit is 3194. On the subject of forced labour, Mr. President, this is a report -- it's a request, excuse me, dated the 5th of July, 1993, for prisoners to be taken to build bunkers between the New Bank and the grammar school on the front line in Mostar. As indicated by the note on this document, the approval for the use of these prisoners was given by Mr. Pusic. Exhibit 4500. 4500 is a list of prisoners from Sovici and Doljani, identifying those who were either taken to labour or were in the hospital for treatment. The list is dated the 25th of August, 1993, and it's directed specifically to Mr. Pusic from Josip Praljak, to inform him about the Sovici, Doljani prisoners. The next -- excuse me. The next exhibit is 3171. Pusic received reports informing him of the extreme danger of the labour that he was sending prisoners to perform, or the labour that he was approving prisoners be taken to perform. Exhibit 3171, this one dated the 4th of July, informs him of a group of prisoners who were taken to work, two of whom were wounded by the BiH army and were transferred to the hospital when they were working. This report was directed to Mr. Pusic as supervising officer, also directed specifically to the chief, Mr. Valentin Coric. The Trial Chamber could also look at Exhibit 3414 regarding prisoners wounded on the 13th of July. Exhibit P 03435, prisoners wounded on the 10th of July. These documents establish that Heliodrom officials informed Pusic and Coric of the fact that wounded prisoners who had been sent for forced labour on Pusic's approval had been wounded. Josip Praljak who signed these reports on behalf of the Heliodrom warden testified that he never received any reaction to his warnings to HVO authorities about the dangers of the forced labour. That's page 14785 of the transcript. The next exhibit is 7498. Mr. President, this is a list sent to Pusic by Mr. Bozic, the Heliodrom warden, on the 6th of January, 1994, identifying 37 prisoners of war and civilians who died during work. The next is Exhibit P 07148. Mr. President, this is an important document. It relates to this and other issues impacting the prisoner and exchange issues. The document is the minutes of a meeting that was chaired by Marijan Biskic on the 11th of December, 1993. Mr. Pusic attended this meeting as well as Mr. Bozic, the Heliodrom warden, and other HVO officials. On page 3 of this document, Mr. President, Pusic identifies all of the detention centres and indicates that he does not have a precise figure on the overall number of detainees because "until now detainees were constantly being taken away to work, mostly on the preparation of the front line." On page 4 Pusic gives figures on the numbers of prisoners at detention centres in Livno, Tomislavgrad, and Gabela. Interestingly, on the same page, in response to a question from Marijan Biskic regarding determining the number of prisoners who were part of the Muslim armed forces, Pusic indicated that there were only five such cases. On page 5 of this document, Mr. President, as the parties were discussing the release of the prisoners, Mr. Pusic said that he was in favour of releasing the prisoners but that they should be prepared "so that they can be sent abroad." Bosnian Muslim prisoners continued to be sent to perform labour in dangerous front-line positions and continued to be killed and wounded while doing so. This practice with the knowledge, approval, and support of Berislav Pusic continued into 1994, and this is shown by the fact that the ICRC sent a letter to Marijan Biskic with a copy to Mr. Pusic pointing out that the ICRC was not able to register or visit numerous prisoners because they had been taken away to perform forced labour. That is Exhibit P 07537. Likewise, as the many orders signed by Pusic and the testimony of Witness E, Nihad Kovac, and Spomenka Drljevic demonstrate, Berislav Pusic, together with Valentin Coric had the authority to order the transfer of prisoners and to regulate where they would be imprisoned. Pusic informed Spomenko Drljevic in person at Ljubuski that she and other female prisoners would be transferred to the Heliodrom. That's page 1050 to 1053 of the transcript. The next exhibit is P 07158. Pusic could prevent the transfer of prisoners when it served the needs of the HVO. In December of 1993, he signed off on a list of detainees from Jablanica who would remain at the Heliodrom because they were needed for an exchange of Croats in Jablanica. Pusic's jurisdiction over prisoners extended to Muslim prisoners wherever they were from. Mr. President, if we could go into private session for one brief moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in public session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That over 400 prisoners would be arriving from Zepce and Zavidovici way up in Central Bosnia and that they would be held at a new makeshift detention facility at Otok, also called Vitina, in Ljubuski municipality. In keeping with his usual practice requiring documentation and lists, Pusic directed Witness E to make a list of the prisoners. Later, the HVO military police transferred another group of around 200 Bosnian Muslims, civilians, from Capljina and detained them also at the Otok/Vitina camp which by this time, according to Witness E had between 6 and 700 prisoners who were held in a place that was nothing more than a concrete slab with a roof over it, no walls, no water, no facilities. According to Witness E and Witness EI, Bosnian Muslim detainees from Otok camp were eventually transferred to the Heliodrom. This would be at transcript pages 22070 for Witness E, and 26139 for EI. We know that at least some of these prisoners were transferred to the Heliodrom on the orders of Berislav Pusic. That order is Exhibit P 05083. It's dated the 15th of September, 1993. Bosnian Muslim civilians and prisoners of war who were arrested in various municipalities under the territorial control of the HVO and detained in Ljubuski prison were transferred to the Heliodrom camp upon the joint orders of Berislav Pusic and Valentin Coric. That would be referring to, among others exhibits P 02546, 2535, 2541. Release of prisoners. We could put up Exhibit P 02332. The evidence clearly establishes that it was the pen of Pusic, as well as that of Valentin Coric, that served as the key to the gaols of Herceg-Bosna. Many orders either refer to releases made on the orders of Pusic or are signed by him personally. Exhibit P 02332, dated the 12th of May, 1993, shows that Pusic had authority to approve the release of prisoners from the Heliodrom after the 9th of May HVO operation and arrest of the Muslim population in Mostar. The next exhibit is 2315. Similarly, Mr. President, this exhibit, dated the 11th of May, 1993, demonstrates that Pusic would review the lists of prisoners, indicating specifically which ones could be released and which ones would have to stay in detention. Witness E testified that whenever an order was received from Mr. Coric or Mr. Pusic to release prisoners, those orders were always carried out. That's page 22089 of the transcript. Ultimately, Pusic showed his authority on matters of detention when under intense international pressure, including pressure exerted by their sponsors in Zagreb, the HVO authorities finally decided to close the HVO prison system in late 1993. As mentioned already, Exhibit P 7148, which is the minutes of the meeting with Marijan Biskic on the 13th of December, 1993, that exhibit establishes Pusic's leading role in devising and implementing the release programme in a way that furthered the objective of removing as many Muslims as possible from the territory of Herceg-Bosna. As he says on page 5 of that document, Pusic agreed that the prisoners should be released but that preparations should be made so that the prisoners could be sent abroad. Mr. President, the Prosecution submits that in addition to his role and involvement in the arrest, detentions, forced labour, and release of prisoners, Berislav Pusic made a substantial contribution to the goals of the joint criminal enterprise in the procedures and practices he advocated for the release of prisoners. The evidence shows that when he said to Marijan Biskic that preparations should be made to send the prisoners abroad, Pusic was describing his own intent in respect of prisoner release and exchange. The evidence shows that when Mr. Pusic released a Bosnian Muslim prisoner, it was his intention, if at all possible, that that prisoner should never return to his home. I have mentioned the testimony of Witness BC regarding the transit visas and the travel documents that were being issued in June of 1993 by HVO authorities. With these documents Muslims in Mostar would sign their property over to the HVO and leave the country. It was Pusic's office that was responsible for the issuance of these documents. Page 18326 of the transcript. Pusic was also part of a working group proposing the relocation of detained individuals and the opening of a transit centre in Ljubuski. That's Exhibit P 03573. Witness BA testified about that transit centre proposed by Mr. Prlic and the HVO from which Muslim prisoners would be deported to third countries. The next exhibit is 3668. Pusic's authority to decide the fate of prisoners and evicted persons was not just limited to those in HVO prisons. Exhibit P 03668 is an inquiry sent from Stipe Pole, who is the commander of the 3rd Battalion, Mijat Tomic in Jablanica. This inquiry is dated the 23rd of July, 1993. He said that during the night some 400 Muslim women, children, and elderly had been brought into the Doljani sector from the direction of Posusje. This HVO unit wanted some guidance as to what they should do with these 400 Muslim women children and elderly. To whom did this HVO battalion commander direct his inquiry? He directed it to Messrs. Coric and Pusic personally. Who responded to this inquiry? We see that in Exhibit P 03652. In a response given on the same day, Pusic told Stipe Pole to escort the Muslims to the last HVO check-point in Doljani and let them walk to Jablanica. Apparently allowing them to return home was not an option for Mr. Pusic, or Mr. Coric, for that matter. The Trial Chamber will recall that Witness CG, a woman arrested by the HVO in her home municipality of Capljina was among those brought to Sovici and then forced to walk to Jablanica at Pusic's direction. Page 10801 of the transcript. By the summer and fall of 1993, the HVO under Valentin Coric and Berislav Pusic began implementation of a large-scale programme whereby prisoners could be released from an HVO prison if they could produce the paperwork and the letters of guarantee to prove that they and their families would leave their homes altogether and move to a third country. As Josip Praljak testified, those prisoners who were able to obtain the required documentation then needed Pusic's signature on behalf of the office of exchange. If they got that, they could be released. That's page 14770 of the transcript. However, the release came at a high price. This deportation scheme was very clearly described by Witness E as it applied -- as it was applied in the Ljubuski municipality. Bosnian Muslim detainees possessing the required paperwork were released and given 24 hours to go home, get their families, and leave for a third country. The Bosnian Muslim houses were then occupied by Croats. This is pages 22101, 22095, 22106, 22184 of the transcript. The exhibits show that Berislav Pusic was aware of and participated in this deportation practice himself. Exhibits P 04450, 7178, 7214. Alija Lizde and Fahrudin Rizvanbegovic, both of whom testified in this case, had papers signed by Pusic authorising their release based on such guarantees. Those are exhibits P 05949 and 7097. Ironically, the Trial Chamber will recall that Mr. Lizde was arrested on the 10th of May, 1993, during the HVO operation at the Vranica headquarters in Mostar. Pusic himself was present when Lizde was arrested. When he asked Pusic why he'd been arrested, Pusic replied that the Armija had arrested some of their men so that they, the HVO, decided to gather a few of us Muslims to have us exchanged. And so it turned out to be Pusic who was directly involved in both the arrest and the eventual release of Alija Lizde some seven months later. Pusic's statement to Alija Lizde that some Muslims were being arrested so that they, the HVO, would have some prisoners to exchange, demonstrates that Pusic saw all the Muslims in HVO territory as potential currency for exchange. He told Witness BC that all the Muslims currently in HVO-controlled areas are valuable to the Croatian Defence Council for use in future exchanges. I'm referring now to Exhibit P 9848, which is under seal, and Exhibit -- or I'm sorry, page number 25207 of the transcript. The next exhibit is P 07102. Mr. President, this exhibit is a proposal for the work of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna service for exchange of captives and other persons. It's dated the 10th of December, 1993, and it was sent by Pusic to Jadranko Prlic personally. In this report on page 5 -- I'm told we don't have it on Sanction. My apologies. On page 5 of this exhibit which is 7102, Pusic states that the prisons are interesting for the service only for the purpose of seeking certain persons for exchange, and therefore we need to specify how the captives to be exchanged are to be taken out, how they are to be checked, and this is to be done in cooperation with the institution in charge of the prisons. To Mr. Pusic the prisons were only interesting to the service, only for the purpose of seeking certain persons for exchange. In informing Jadranko Prlic of the work and the recommendations of the service for exchange, whether as to Muslim POWs, civilians, those in prison, those otherwise being held in preventive isolation, Pusic played a key role in shaping HVO policy in respect of prisoners and prisoner exchange issues. Mr. President, I don't know that I can finish. Are we going until 10.30? I'm sorry. Then I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. You have 20 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Amor Masovic was a member of the BiH State commission for the exchange of prisoners of war and persons deprived of liberty. He told the Trial Chamber that Mr. Pusic told him and other members of the international community, like the ICRC, that all men between 18 and 65 years of age are soldiers and that they should all be in camps or prisons. That's at page 25032 of the transcript. This statement by Mr. Pusic clearly reflected HVO policy and practice. Mr. Masovic testified further that the other practice which Pusic implemented and advocated publicly was that "all Croatians who lived on the territory not under HVO control were potential prisoners." Pusic told Masovic that it was his task to see that those people were transferred from that territory, the territory where they were potential prisoners, to territory under the control of the Croatian Defence Council. Thus, and not surprisingly, we see evidence that Pusic supported the practice of reverse ethnic cleansing that the Trial Chamber has heard about in these proceedings from various witnesses and the ECMM in particular. If we could go briefly into private session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It is important for us all to recall, Mr. President, exactly what Mr. Pusic was advocating when he said that the Muslims in Western Herzegovina should be sent to East Mostar where they belong. Within two weeks of this conversation between Pusic and Witness BC, Jeremy Bowen and a BBC film crew managed to reach East Mostar, and they filmed the documentary is now in evidence as Exhibit 6365. I would like to show the Trial Chamber a brief three-minute excerpt of that film just so that as we sit here in this courtroom today all these years and miles away from East Mostar at that time, we can all recall precisely what "sending them to the east bank" meant in September of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm not hearing any audio, Mr. President. Could we stop this until we get the audio fixed. [Videotape played]. "THE NARRATOR: Bosnian soldiers told them which way -- it gets no better at night. Five hundred Muslims have just been robbed and thrown out of their homes in West Mostar by the Croats. They had to cross the river Neretva to get to comparative safety on a bridge made of ropes and planks. Bosnian soldiers told them which way to go. "The Croats were shooting at the people they just made refugees. Only a few hours before until the Croat gangs had come for them and forced them over the front line they thought they were safe. They'd been settling down for the night. "The Croat machine-guns didn't let up and the refugees kept on coming. They were trying to kill old men and women, mothers and their children. "She was so frightened she could barely walk, but she tried to calm her sons. "Each new family has to be fed and housed. This is a war crime with a cold purpose, to increase the pressure on the military authorities in East Mostar. And the brutality of the expulsions writes home the message that compromise with Croat extremists is neither possible nor desirable. "The refugees spent their first night in East Mostar in a bombed-out theatre. In one evening all of them had lost their homes and possessions. They talked of persecution, rape, and murder. "We were driven to a small wood. My sons were pulled out of the car. They were taken into that wood. I was told that their throats were slit. I only live because I have to. Only because I have to. What sort of life is this?"

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, it is impossible that Berislav Pusic, being who he was and where he was, did not know about the expulsions of Muslims that were taking place in his own town and throughout Western Herzegovina. His statement to Witness BC unequivocally voicing his support for the ethnic cleansing campaign in Mostar makes clear his support and his intention to contribute to the joint criminal enterprise which had as its very purpose the conduct that we've just watched on the screens. The evidence summarised, Mr. President, in these submissions clearly establishes Mr. Pusic's own contribution to that joint criminal enterprise. Mr. President, as counsel for Mr. Pusic pointed out in his submissions, Mr. Pusic did not personally commit every crime with which he's charged. The Defence argues that there is no evidence linking Mr. Pusic, for example, to the rapes and sexual assaults charged in counts 4 and 5, or to the perpetrators of those crimes. The Defence argues that there is no evidence linking Pusic to the crimes and perpetrators who committed the crimes of extensive destruction, unlawful attacks on the civilians in Mostar, and terror, for example. It is clear that the role and the contribution of Mr. Pusic to this criminal -- joint criminal enterprise and the crimes that he did personally commit in furtherance of it related not to destruction, military operations, and rapes committed by individual soldiers. Pusic's role related to the prisoners and the civilians, using them for forced labour and the procedures and the practices that he employed to ultimately bring about their departure from HVO territory in the so-called Herceg-Bosna. As a willing and contributing member of the joint criminal enterprise, Mr. Pusic is criminally responsible for the crimes committed by others who were making their own different contribution to the aim of the joint criminal enterprise when crimes such as destruction, terror, and even rape became a part of the JCE or certainly were a foreseeable consequence of it. And so, Mr. President, it is our submission that the Prosecution has submitted ample evidence to show that by his own acts and conduct, by his omissions and failure to take any reasonable measures to prevent crimes directed against prisoners, and by virtue of his own substantial contribution to the aims of the joint criminal enterprise, Mr. Pusic is criminally responsible for all of the counts with which he's charged in the indictment. And that's the conclusion of my submissions, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It is now 20 minutes past 10.00. It is better to have a 20-minute break now, and we shall reconvene in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have resumed our hearing. Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, each of Your Honours, Counsel, all those in and around the courtroom who are assisting us. Mr. President, Your Honours, before I make my submission, the Prosecution's submission concerning the accused Coric, let me just come back on a couple of things from yesterday to make a couple of corrections and one note, hopefully that will be helpful to Your Honours. In using the -- some of the presidential transcript material yesterday, while we have tried and tried over and over again to avoid duplicate numbers, I'm afraid that sometimes they still creep back into the system or when people use different tools for purposes of preparation. I made referenced yesterday to an exhibit by the number of P 01594. That is a duplicate of -- it's the exact same evidence, but it's a duplicate of P 01622. So the correct exhibit number for that evidence should be P 01622. And in a similar fashion, I made reference to an exhibit P 04759, which is a duplicate of P 08448, which is the correct number for that evidence. I've also been alerted to a third item that we are still checking on, but -- and we'll come back to the Chamber or the legal officers and registry when we've determined that. The Chamber yesterday, I made a couple of comments and I think, Mr. President, you in terms of being able to put more of the exhibits on the screen, and I commend of course Mr. Stringer and his use of that material which I hope assisted the Chamber, in particular with regard to the presidential transcript material which everyone will know that I made frequent reference to yesterday. I do think that's important evidence, obviously, and I would just remind the Judges just only out of an attempt to be helpful that the admitted excerpts of the presidential transcripts with some adjustments based on the Chamber's actual rulings, there might have been a sentence out here or a page added or deleted there, but 99 per cent with some adjustments that are needed, that material can all be found in annex 3 to the Prosecution's 26 October 2007 motion to admit presidential transcript evidence. All of that -- all the excerpts that been admitted into addition to the other admitted material through witnesses can be found in that set of materials. In terms of the Accused Valentin Coric, I hope the Chamber will find these missions helpful. Once again, of course, as Mr. Stringer said again today, we are focusing for the purposes of these submissions, of course, on counts, not on specific crime base, and we are focusing for purposes of these submissions on the existence and operation of a joint criminal enterprise and Mr. Coric's membership in that enterprise and his substantial contributions to it. Once again, we will not be specifically addressing other modes of liability. I will not be discussing in my submissions, for example, 7(3), responsibility, because again it's the Prosecution's submission that at the end of these proceedings, that is the 98 bis proceedings, there is more than substantial and indeed the Prosecution would submit compelling evidence that all the counts should survive as each of the six accused in the case going forward. And I'll try to be slower today and be mindful of that, although I'm not confident I'll be successful. We submit, Your Honours, that the totality of the Prosecution evidence shows that Mr. Coric, in his ongoing senior position in the HVO structure apparatus and processes, establishes both his de jure and de facto powers and abilities to affect and influence events and the conduct in particular of the HVO military police, and plainly demonstrates and give rise, if nothing else, to the clear inference of his knowledge of the conflict and the ethnic policies and strategies with which he was involved and with which he was confronted on a virtually -- must have been on a virtually day-to-day basis. I might just note on that point in general, not only as to Mr. Coric, but as terms of these events, Your Honours, as -- in a very real sense we have to remember that the area that we're talking about, Herceg-Bosna, was a small geographic area. These events took place over a substantial period of time. And the Chamber, with respect, must consider, in terms of considering the knowledge and notice of each of the accused, that these were substantial, horrific events taking place in a small geographic area over a long period of time, and the Prosecution submits it is virtually impossible that most people in this area, let alone these six highly placed persons, could not and would not have been aware of all these events and developments. Again, as I said in my comments yesterday, we did not really hear -- at least I did not understand the Coric Defence to dispute so much the crime base as to the conclusions to be drawn from the Prosecution evidence as to Mr. Coric's responsibility for what happened, so there again we will not be discussing the crime base in any detail. We can start by looking once again at the presidential transcript evidence where Mr. Coric, as the other -- most of the other accused also feature. In Exhibit P 02099, a meeting and set of conversations on the 26th of April, 1993, there is discussion again of what's happening. Susak, Tudjman, and others, both Franjo Tudjman and his son Miroslav Tudjman, who also played a senior role in the Tudjman government at that time, either formally or informally. And in that meeting Mr. Coric comes up and -- comes up as a topic, and Miroslav Tudjman takes the credit, Mr. Tudjman, Franjo Tudjman's son, for appointing Valentin Coric as the head of military police, which in itself is an interesting concept that it would be someone in Croatia appointing -- that it would be someone in Croatia appointing the head of the military police in Herceg-Bosna. On page 23 of that exhibit, the conversation goes on, President Tudjman speaking: "I cannot remember that now. I lost the contact with him for some time. The reason that they put him in the same context with Valentin Coric is because they knew each other as sportsmen. They were in my club at the same time," Franjo Tudjman says. "Valentin Coric was appointed in the month of October in 1992 at the time when that centre had not yet been operational. Valentin was brought then and he was practically in charge ever since. I have there maybe 10 more persons who were in my club as sportsmen." Then continuing back Mr. Coric comes up again on page 38 of the meeting and Susak says: "It is too much, President. From what I heard from him, it is too much that he talks about Valentin Coric." President: "Valentin is -- he knows him for 20 years now. Valentin is the chief of the military police in Herceg-Bosna. If anything works in that part then it is that military police. Miroslav Tudjman: "I recommended him. Susak: "Miro," for Miroslav Tudjman, "Miro recommended him." Your Honours, the job description if you will of Mr. Coric as the chief of the military police administration is summarised in the book of regulations on the systematization of duties in the HVO military police administration, which is Exhibit P 00978. The chief of the military police administration managed and organised the work of the military police administration. He commanded, oversaw, monitored, coordinated, controlled, all military police units, including battalions in the operative zones and another set of units that were formed at one point in time called light assault battalions, which were also part -- for a time part of the military police structure. He conducted business by cooperating, of course, with other organs and services of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna and HVO. He conducted the personnel policies in the military police and decided on all major issues, all major policies, all major strategies related to the work of the HVO military police. In terms of some of the de jure evidence, of course the legal provisions concerning the HVO military police responsibilities are found in the various official Herceg-Bosna documentation, including that published in the Narodni List, and there is a great deal of that material in the Trial Record. Under these enactments, the HVO military police was considered part of the military forces under the command of the HVO department or Ministry of Defence. One of the basic applicable laws is the decree on the armed forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which is Exhibit P 00588. Article 137 of that decree provides: "The armed forces including military police who take charge of security in military traffic, military order and discipline, and elimination of criminal elements in the armed forces." And I'll come back to that perhaps in a moment, but I think that bears a pause. "The elimination of criminal elements in the armed forces." If there was one part of the HVO which by law and by function should have been involved in policing HVO crimes and misconduct, not only generally but specifically in connection with the crimes against Muslims, it should have been the military police. That was indeed one of the very specific de jure responsibilities of the military police as stated in various of the HVO military police documents. We also have the temporary guidelines for work of military police units of the HVO, which can be found at Exhibit P 00143. In November 1992, these guidelines were amended and some parts were expanded. The guidelines state that the military police administration was set up as part of the HVO and was in charge of all units of the military police which were part of the operative zones, the organisational units, and the military police administration. In those guidelines it specifically states that all members of the military police were required to know its provisions and instructions concerning the work of the military police. The members of the military police in pursuit of their duties and in executing their orders were to follow the provisions of these guidelines and other regulations, respecting at all times integrity and dignity of HVO members and "other citizens." Again, that can be found at Exhibit P 00837. That same document sets out the particularly important functions and responsibilities or duties of the military police as follows: The protection of property -- excuse me, the protection of people and property in the zone of responsibility of a specific operation zone and other units on a specific territory. Two, respect for military order, discipline, and prescribed security measures. Three, the detection of crimes and finding the perpetrator of a crime in cases when crimes were committed by HVO members or in connection with property and facilities belonging to the HVO. Number four, providing security for high-ranking military officers, documents, combat means, with the highest level of secrecy, sectors, zones, access, and military facilities of special importance for the HVO and the country's defence. Five, ensuring the internal security of military prisons and premises where detained persons are held. Six, participating in channeling the direction of movement, the direction of movement of refugees and uncovers members of enemy units infiltrating among -- infiltrated among refugees. Number seven participates in providing security for prisoners of war. Now, that is not my summary but that is as set out in Exhibit P 08837. One of the important features that Mr. Coric was involved in, of course, is -- was the training and equipping of the military police. That is set out in a number of exhibits. I'll just mention a few because I'm not going to spend a lot of time on this particular part, but you can find evidence of that in Exhibit P 00423, P 00475, P 00509, P 00864. And I'll stop there for these purposes. In one of those, in fact, in Exhibit P 00475, that is a communication from Valentin Coric as chief of the military police on 14 September 1992, writing to his superior, Bruno Stojic, seeking Stojic's approval for the military police training centre located in Neum. Coric in his letter to Stojic seeking his approval, Coric stressed that: "In the period ahead," and this is September 1992, "In the period ahead, the military police will have to carry out very complex and responsible task aimed at establishing full control over the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." Coric explained to Stojic at that time that he already had 100 active-duty military policemen ready for training, and also indicated that this training and the programme had also been set up and would be supported by instructors from the Republic of Croatia. Exhibit P 01629 is another Valentin Coric order, this time the 8th of March, 1993, again concerning military police training issued to all military police commanders. And in terms of that component of his responsibilities, we will leave the evidence to that -- at that. The reporting system followed by the HVO military police shows that really as was the case throughout the HVO, we've heard at times that there were -- that there weren't effective communication systems, that it was difficult to reach people, undoubtedly that was true at times. I mean, I don't think any of us can say in a conflict, wartime situation that there wouldn't have been moments when there probably was a communications system problem somewhere, but what the evidence shows and what various Prosecution witnesses have indicated, including again General Pringle, who assessed the situation, there was indeed an effective communication and reporting system up and down the chain of command. The Chamber has seen numerous documents evidencing what can only be considered realtime communication. Reports, new orders, reports, new orders. Do this today, report back an hour later. There was an effective communication system. And the ability to reach people, I think, was interestingly demonstrated in perhaps a bit humourous way but nonetheless in a very real way when Witness DZ was even actually -- was able to show us that he still had the telephone numbers for Mr. Pusic and Mr. Prlic on his telephone even now. He said, "I never had a problem reaching them when I needed to." The HVO military police reporting was likewise well-established, functioned well. There was a series of, as in most again the rest of the organisation of the HVO, monthly, weekly, daily reports dealing with a wide array of issues such as border control and check-points, arrest, confiscation of vehicles, securing of detention facilities, and transfer of prisoners, as well as the regular activities of military police units. One exhibit illustrating that is Exhibit P 01788. On the 7th of April, 1993 --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting my colleague, but I don't know whether there was a misunderstanding because it's not in the transcript, and those of us listening to the B/C/S, Croatian, the interpretation we got was that Witness DZ said that he had the telephone number of Mr. Coric and Mr. Pusic. Witness DZ in his testimony didn't mention Mr. Coric's telephone number at all. Now, I wasn't listening to the original -- to Mr. Scott in English. So I don't know what names he actually said, but just in case, I wanted to raise that objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the moment I honestly don't recall myself. If I misspoke, the record is clear and my memory is clear, having been alerted by counsel, the numbers that were referred to were those of Jadranko Prlic and Berislav Pusic. If I said Coric a moment ago, my apologies. I don't think I did but in any event, I hope that's corrected. I was referring to just now Exhibit P 01821. On the 7th of April, 1993, Mr. Coric issued instructions addressed to the commanders of the military police organisation, the Police Battalions, instructing them to submit daily and weekly reports to the military police administration, be it by fax, paket communication, or telephone. All HVO military police battalions were to submit their weekly reports to the military police administration. In fact, monthly reports were supposed to be submitted by the fifth day of each month. An HVO military police report dated the 26th of December 1992 P 00956 states and confirms that indeed regular reports were received from the battalions. Suffice it to say that both Witness C and Witness E talked about the reporting -- the reporting system in the military police and gave testimony that is consistent with the evidence that I have just outlined to the Chamber. We also have the evidence that the warden at the Heliodrom, Stanko Bozic, reported directly to Coric. That was in particular again in the evidence of Witness C, and I think there was other evidence of that from the Witness Josip Praljak and others. We'll come back in the course of our submission to Mr. Coric and the HVO camps and prisons a bit later. Mr. President, Your Honours, the evidence shows that the military police of the HVO were involved in virtually, if not literally, every aspect of the HVO operation in one fashion or another, every aspect and dimension of the joint criminal enterprise, and was a necessary and important cog, if you will, or part, in the HVO machinery. Indeed, the HVO machinery probably wouldn't have worked without it, the military police. They were involved in Prozor in October 1992. Coric himself in Exhibit P 01635 says that 100 HVO military policemen participated in Prozor operation. On Prozor you also -- the Chamber can also refer to this evidence: Exhibit P 00608, Exhibit P 00612, Exhibit P 00647, Exhibit P 00712, Exhibit P 00716, Exhibit P 00744. And I'll refer to Exhibit P 00956, which I mentioned yesterday, which is again Valentin Coric's own report as chief of the military police for all of the work of the HVO military police from the time of its foundation in April 1992 to the end of December 1992. If the Chamber wants to look at one single exhibit summarising and setting out a great deal of information as to the functioning of the military police from April to December 1992, it is Mr. Coric's own report, Exhibit P 00956. In that report, in connection now with Prozor, Mr. Coric says, and I actually referred to this yesterday but I'll briefly refer to it again now: "On 23 October 1992, there was an armed clash between members of the BH army and the HVO in Prozor and military police units intervened. Within a short time, the town was under the control of the military police. On the military police side, one member was killed and five were wounded." The next exhibit that I'll refer to -- the Chamber to for the purposes of demonstrating the military police's operation -- operational involvement in Prozor is Exhibit P 00836. It's an order by Mr. Coric on the 30th of November, after the conflict but talking about the regrouping of military police units in Prozor following the conflict in October. There is also evidence, Your Honours, that the chief of military police had knowledge of crimes committed in Prozor municipality, including by military police members but failed to take necessary measures to prevent those crimes or to punish the perpetrators. The commander of the 2nd Battalion military police, Zedenko Andabak, reported to Mr. Coric about the events in Prozor in his report which is Exhibit P 00536. That report, among other things, details the looting and destruction of Muslim property. According to a similar report which is Exhibit P 00721, dated 8 November 1992, a few days after the events, the HVO military police did nothing to restore order in Prozor after the conflict on 23, 24 October. We move to Gornji Vakuf in January 1993. Here again the HVO military police played a major role in those events. In a report that month which is Exhibit P 01053, Mr. Coric, again himself, confirmed to Bruno Stojic that the military police units had been active at Gornji Vakuf. And at one point there had been at the forward command post in Gornji Vakuf municipality the HVO military police had been involved in that. Indeed, Your Honours, it's interesting to note that in those very important series of orders on the 15th of January, 1993, and remember we have the Jadranko Prlic decision, the ultimatum, implemented by Bruno Stojic's order, implemented by Petkovic's order, all issued on the 15th of January, 1993. And in the Stojic order, which is Exhibit P 01140, who does Stojic say is responsible for carrying out that ultimatum? "The chief of the Main Staff of the armed forces of the HVO and the chief of the HVO military police administration shall be responsible to me for the implementation of this order." Stojic to Valentin Coric. "You carry out this ultimatum, and you're responsible to me for doing so." The witness Andrew Williams testified to participating in meetings during January 1993 at which the participation of the HVO military police in these operations was discussed. And that can be found in the transcripts starting at page 8506. Williams recalled a specific incident where the military police cleansed the village of Hrasnica, attacking it three times. According to Williams, each attack was worse than the previous one. Eventually the village was totally destroyed. That action which became particularly notorious, was brought up during the cease-fire negotiations which followed and in which Mr. Williams was involved, and there was no denial by the HVO representatives at that meeting that it was their forces who had cleansed and destroyed that village, and there was no denial by the HVO representatives that it was the HVO military police who had done it. That part of Mr. Williams' testimony can be found starting at transcript page 8507. Exhibit P 03090, which again is another helpful document to the Chamber, we submit, is Coric's further report on the work of the HVO military police for the first half of 1993. So if you want a summary, you have the previous exhibit I referred you to a few moments ago which covers all of April to December 1992. Exhibit P 03090 is Mr. Coric's own report that covers the first six months of 1993. In that report in giving -- in giving a discussion about what the military police had been involved in Mr. Coric again confirms himself that they were at Gornji Vakuf in January 1993. Turning to Sovici, Doljani, April 1993. The HVO military police were also involved in HVO operations in and around Sovici, Doljani. A report by the military police commander Ilija Franjic, on the 17th -- or for the 17th of April, 1993, which is Exhibit P 01952, indicates, for example, that an HVO military police unit, in cooperation with units of the HVO Rama Brigade, captured 30 Muslims, three of whom were wounded. It says that the plan for further operations on April -- on 18 April was agreed with the OZ, the operative zone commander Siljeg and the Rama Brigade command. Cooperation with other HVO units was regarded as "excellent." The same report from Mr. Franjic, Exhibit P 01952, states that three squads of HVO military police successfully raided and mopped up four Muslim villages, Parcani, Paros, Klek, and Skrobucani on the previous day. An interesting aside connecting to another accused, as part of the operations around Sovici, Doljani, there was specific reference in Exhibit P 10356 in the testimony of witness Hasan Rizvic, that Mr. Berislav Pusic was part of the HVO military police delegation which participated in the HVO ABiH negotiations on those matters. Turning to Mostar, Mr. President, the evidence would show that in virtually at all times and in every aspect the military police played a prominent role in the events in Mostar throughout the period covered by the indictment. During that time, for example, the HVO military police was ordered to increase security in and around Mostar, even back as early as October of 1992. And again I referred to that evidence yesterday, that with the conflict and tension around Novi Travnik and Prozor in October 1992, orders were given to Coric to increase the security level, if you will, around Mostar at the same time and to take control of various facilities in Mostar in October 1992. The post office building, the MUP building, the police station, the radio station, all taken over and secured by the HVO military police, which can be found in Exhibit P 00619. Once again, Exhibit P 03090, the Coric report on the first half of 1993, once again he confirms extensive military police involvement in Mostar, specifically including the operations on the 9th and 10th of May, 1993. The Chamber will recall, and I'm not going to go into detail for these purposes, but the Chamber will recall that one of the HVO military police base of operations, one might consider perhaps depending on your point of view, famous or infamous or notorious, was the mechanical engineering factory the very place where many of the Muslim men taken from the Vranica building on the 10th of May 1993 went missing. That was a military police facility. And in fact, there were numerous instances throughout the Prosecution evidence of people being talked about, various witnesses, and I won't go into them all now because -- well, a couple by example. Mustafa Hadrovic, Alija Lizde, several others; Witness CV. All gave accounts of being taken at various times and receiving various treatment at the mechanical engineering faculty. P 02601, in terms of again demonstrating Mr. Coric's and the military police's involvement and responsibilities in connection with Mostar, that exhibit is a letter from ICRC to Mr. Coric dated the 1st of June, 1993, requesting a meeting, an immediate meeting, to discuss, among other things, providing food, sanitation, and medical aid to East Mostar, and makes the statement, and this is even -- this is the 1st of June, 1993, and ICRC states: "According to multiple assessments of the situation by our physician and sanitation engineer, the hygienic conditions are rapidly deteriorating (risk of epidemics) and the provision of food for the entire population has been made more difficult due to the isolation of this part of the city." And the additional significance of that letter is that when ICRC was reaching out to someone to address this matter, who did they go to? Who did they send their letter to? Valentin Coric, requesting an immediate meeting to address these issues. Exhibit P 04174 is an order by Valentin Coric dated the 13th of August, 1993, to the 5th Battalion military police, which confirms both a higher-up orders and his own order to the following effect: "Pursuant to the order of the HVO Main Staff of 13 August 1993, I hereby order entrance into Mostar is forbidden to all persons until otherwise ordered. The order pertains to all foreign journalists and TV crews. The ban does not pertain to HVO members. The commanders of the 5th Battalion of the military police and companies shall be responsible to me, Valentin Coric, for carrying out this order." Mr. Coric controlled access to Mostar. Gave an order entrance into Mostar is forbidden, in particular to foreign journalists and TV crews. Exhibit P 02853 is a report from Stanko Bozic, the warden of the Heliodrom on the 19th of June, 1993, that on the 9th of May, 1993, 1.820 "displaced persons" had been detained at the Heliodrom, Mr. Bozic seeing fit to report that up his chain of command to Mr. Coric. Turning to other general -- more general, perhaps, other HVO military operations during this time covered by the indictment, we can just look at a few examples. On the 9th of June, 1993, the commander of the north-west operative zone, Siljeg, informed Mate Boban, Bruno Stojic, Milivoj Petkovic, and Valentin Coric of HVO military police misconduct in the Prozor and Gornji Vakuf municipalities. That can be found at Exhibit P 02911. A few weeks later, on the basis of a 22 June 1993 order by Milivoj Petkovic, Coric sent military police as reinforcements to Prozor on 28 June 1993. P 03057 is a report from the commander of the 3rd Company, 3rd Battalion military police, to the military police administration giving its report for the 30th of June and the 1st of July, 1993, by the Capljina military police. "Pursuant to the order by the 1st HVO Knez Domagoj Brigade on bringing in Muslim men liable for military service which resulted from the deterioration of the security situation caused by the events in Mostar, 161 persons were taken in and brought to the Dretelj military compound in the period between the entry into force of this order," and I went through those series of orders again yesterday starting with the Stojic and Prlic decision and order at the top in disseminating down the HVO chain of command, and we have this specific report in the military police, "161 persons were taken in and brought to Dretelj between the entry into force of this order and 1 July at 0700 hours." P 03075 is another work -- is another document, a report again from the 3rd Battalion HVO military police.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I referred to this one yesterday, and it again gives a full account of the involvement of three different -- at least three different military police platoons which were part of the 3rd Battalion in gathering up the Muslim -- as described here as "persons of Muslim faith" in the Stolac, Neum, and surrounding areas. Exhibit P 03307 is to similar effect. Exhibit P 03971, a SIS report for the Rama Brigade, dated 5 August 1993, again gives an account of the military police's involvement in bringing in Muslim men between age 16 and 60. It says specifically that. "The Security Information Service, the SIS, and the military police acting according to and carrying out the order from a higher level for Muslims aged between 16 and 60 to be brought in." It also notes that there had in fact been some instances of some men over 60 and under 16 also collected, caught up in the net, if you will, and that report goes on to specifically ask for direction: "What do you want us to do? What do we do with those over 60 and those under 16?" Asking for direction. Exhibit P 09994 is an ECMM report for 1 September 1993 describing the involvement of HVO military police in the north-west operative zone around Prozor in the collection of approximately 2.000 Muslims. The Prosecution evidence, Your Honours, also shows, in addition to that already outlined, the involvement of the military police in eviction of Muslims from their homes and the forcible transfer of Muslims. In the similar -- in a conversation that I also made reference to yesterday, Witness BC indicated that he had met with HVO officials, including Valentin Coric, specifically raising the issue of ethnic cleansing and expulsion of Muslims in Mostar, in Capljina, and in Ljubuski. And Witness BC indicated that, well, although Mr. Coric was always very businesslike and always promised to do something, he never did. No protection of the Muslims ever materialised. And that can be found at transcript 18340 to 18344. The witness Anton van der Grinten had a meeting on the 16th of June, 1993, with both Coric and Berislav Pusic concerning the expulsion of Muslims from West Mostar and the situation at the Heliodrom. Witness E gave evidence that in June 1993, Croat refugees, Croat refugees from various regions of Bosnia and Herzegovina, were accommodated first in primary school building in Ljubuski and then later moved into houses that previously had been inhabited by Muslims. At the end of August 1993, the Muslims living in the wholly -- what had been the Muslim village of Gradska in Ljubuski municipality were forced simply to leave their homes, lock them, leave the keys and move on. That can be found at transcript pages 22105, 22074, 22097, 22103, 22104. Exhibit P 02802 is a report from the 1st Company, 3rd Battalion, HVO military police, for the 15th of June, 1993, in Mostar. And this is one trying to make some effort to emulate my superior colleague Mr. Stringer, I do have one item that I can put up at least now on the screen for you from Exhibit 2802. First slide. 2802. In the report of that day, military police report under the section titled "Crime" here's this language: "No criminal acts or incidents were notified yesterday. Only the ethnic cleansing of the town from persons of Muslim nationality was noticed. The perpetrators of this act are the members of the 4th Battalion and members of the anti-terrorist group ATG Baja Kraljevic."
