I think,, Your Honours, I submit that speaks volumes over the mind-set and the attitude, the policy of the HVO. Look at that again. "No criminal acts were notified yesterday." No criminal acts, no incidents, only the ethnic cleansing of Muslims. Not even considered a crime. Not even considered an important incident, just par for the course. HVO military police. P 04177 is a report from the SIS of the Rama Brigade dated 14 August 1993, which gives an extensive account of crimes committed by the military police against Muslims in that region. The entire document goes on. It's at length. I won't take the time to read it. I ask the Chamber to specifically pull that exhibit, P 04177, and talk -- and read that document. It talks about specifically the entire Muslim population from Rama or Prozor municipality as of the mid-August being placed in three collection centres under the control of the military police, the Muslims being robbed, Muslim women and children -- women and girls being taken out of the collection centres on a daily basis to be raped, abused and humiliated. Men go into Muslim homes and daughters are stripped naked in front of their fathers and vice versa. "All this has been happening systematically for a considerable time now, even though we informed the HVO president Mijo Jozic, their brigade commander, and the commanders of the military and civilian police of this in writing." And the report goes on to show that one of the problems in getting any sort of satisfaction or resolution is they can't turn to the military police because it's the military police that are involved in doing it. That's set out specifically in the report. "Thus the security service is unable to deal with all matters because collaboration with the military police concerning the prevention of such things is impossible given that they are the perpetrators among them." And there's even more, the military police being involved in theft, seized vehicles from humanitarian aid convoys. The military police commander openly admits that he authorised the plunder of the convoy. And an interesting note at the end of the report: "The civilian police," the civilian police, "are unable to cope with all this, and recently they have been mostly in the field under the command of General Slobodan Praljak." The civilian police. As I mentioned earlier one the principal responsibility of the HVO military police, indeed I dare say for the military police of any army or any military force, is to investigate crime committed by members of that army or armed force, which presumably I take it, as I say, in most armies. As I said some minutes ago, surely, surely if there was one component of the HVO that should have been involved in investigating preventing and stopping HVO crimes, including crimes against Muslims, it should have been the HVO military police. As indicated in part by some of the documents, exhibits that I just have referred you to, it was the unfortunate situation that not only did the HVO military police frequently not intervene, not stop and carry out the protection of the civilian population, in particular the Muslim population, but unfortunately many of the most notorious crimes and the worst misconduct was carried out by the military police themselves. I refer the Chamber again to P 01966 and P 02169. I will pause on P 02961, which is a report from the HVO military police in the south-east operative zone, which included the area of Mostar and was under the command of Miljenko Lasic, but this is from the military police. Report for 2 June, 1993: "For Mr. Coric." "The following activities were carried out in Capljina municipality last month," monthly report. "The cargo of a Tuzla-bound convoy consisting mainly of food was seized. The convoy had previously gone through customs in Doljani and was then stopped in Pocitelj before being turned back by the brigade police and sent to the Grabovina barracks where its cargo and vehicles were confiscated." It goes on then also to report: "Members of the brigade police bring in civilians and search their houses and seize items and vehicles from them without issuing them with certificates confirming the seizure thereof. A large number of vehicles and loaded trucks were confiscated during a train search in Gubavica with no certificates, records, or any concrete report issued about all this." And I will also refer the Chamber to Exhibit P 02697, also P 03458, reporting on mistreatment of Muslims in Prozor by HVO military police members and the failure by the military police administration to take appropriate measures. Also Exhibit P 03516. Also Exhibit P 04058, a report in early August that not only went to Coric but also went to Bruno Stojic, again detailing "bringing in the persons of Muslim ethnicity," and noting that most of crimes connected -- excuse me, committed in connection with bringing in "persons of Muslim ethnicity" are crimes against property, with the situation being particularly bad in Capljina and Ljubuski. Goods have been seized and taken to the Dretelj barracks. Vidovic, the author of that document, suggests a number of steps that had to be taken to resolve the problem of crime. I refer the Chamber to Exhibit P 04161, again a SIS report dated the 13th of August, 1993. Again, it detail -- in detail setting out many, many problems involving the military police in that region. In part, Exhibit P 04161 provides or states: "Some military policemen and Rama Brigade members have been coming to the above-named villages to mistreat the populations, take material goods from them, jewellery and money, take young girls away, rape them, and force them into prostitution. There have also been several murders of persons of Muslim nationality. HVO military police from Prozor under the command of Ilija Franjic knew all about the aforementioned offences but has done nothing to prevent them. On the contrary, most of the military police, starting with the commander who behaves as some kind of a 'local sheriff,' are themselves perpetrators of various criminal offences and acts." Just as an aside on another item involved in this case, in that same report, P 04161, the following additional information is provided: "Following initial defeats," excuse me. "Following initial defeats and losses of certain positions, the line is stabilised and the situation is now much improved." And I pause to say this is a report for 13 August, 1993. 13 August. "The situation is now much improved, particularly since units from other parts of the HZ HB have arrived and a part of the 5th Guards Brigade of the HV," the Croatian army. I will additionally refer the Chamber to Exhibits P 06805, which is a report by Radoslav Ravlic. I believe -- in fact, I believe it is the same exhibit that was referred to by Mr. Stringer earlier this morning, his report on the 26th -- excuse me, the 22nd November 1993, which once again, in our submission, provides a helpful summary, if you will, or synopsis of a number of important issues related to the military police, their involvement with the camps, their responsibilities, the fact they were under the command, of course, of Valentin Coric. Also mentions Berislav Pusic's direct involvement. All that set out, among other things, in Exhibit P 06805, dated the 22nd of November, 1993. One interesting statement in that -- one of many interesting statements, actually, paragraph point 10: "We are not acquainted with documentation pertaining to prisoners of war (many were taken in for security reasons)." Here's the new head of military police administration, the successor to Mr. Coric says, "We don't really know the situation of these prisoners. We don't really have any documentation about where they came from or why, except many were taken in for 'security reasons.'" Mr. Coric and the HVO prisons and camps, this topic I turn to. I'll try to take it somewhat quickly. There are a number of exhibits which again make it very clear that Mr. Coric was responsible for, was the man in charge of the Heliodrom camp, with the warden Stanko Bozic frequently reporting to him directly on problems and difficulties and various events taking place at the Heliodrom. I would refer the Chamber to Exhibits P 00292, P 00352, P 00956, P 00513, the operating instructions, if you will, for the Heliodrom prepared and signed by Mr. Coric himself in September 1992. As I think Mr. Stringer also referred to, witness Alija Lizde talked about being collected and taken to the Heliodrom, and their movement, the fact that Muslim men and the mass arrests that started on the 30th of June were collected and taken to the Heliodrom, and this was all done under the auspices and control of the HVO military police. It is significant, Mr. President, Your Honours, that Mate Boban himself, Boban, considered the chief of police -- the chief of the military police as the senior HVO official who was in charge of and responsible for conditions at the Heliodrom. According to the witness van der Grinten in the Trial record starting at page 21028 continuing to page 21031, Mr. Van der Grinten talks about an ECMM delegation desiring to gain access to the Heliodrom and requesting the permission and approval first from Berislav Pusic. The conditions at the camp they found were poor. As to any discussions about the conditions, the Heliodrom warden, Mr. Bozic, refers the ECMM leader to Valentin Coric -- he says if you really want to talk about this, the people you have to talk about are Valentin Coric, Berislav Pusic, and Bruno Stojic. Josip Praljak also commented on Exhibit P 03209, which is his report -- one of his many reports that the Chamber will recall, many exhibits were put in front of Mr. Praljak, Josip Praljak, where he would say, "I sent these reports up the chain of command all the time. I was saying we have these problems, and I was not getting any satisfaction." One of those is Exhibit P 03209. Coming back down, if you will, the chain of command is Exhibit P 05792, a personal handwritten order by Mate Boban directing Coric to take essential measures to improve conditions at the Heliodrom. "Clean up your act, Coric." That the administration of the Heliodrom detention facility was itself under HVO military police administration is further confirmed, if further confirmation is needed, as testified by Josip Praljak that the administrative unit at the prison was considered to be part of the 1st Company, 5th Battalion military police. I would also refer the Chamber to Exhibit P 03551 indicating Mr. Coric's control over access to the Heliodrom, telling the north-west operative zone that we already have too many people there. Don't send any more people to us right now. Paraphrasing. Refer the Chamber to another example of the reports not only from Josip Praljak but also from the warden Stanko Bozic, Exhibit P 03942. Also Exhibit P 05008. That is one where Stanko Bozic -- excuse me, a report in September 1993 again informs Coric of a number of the continuing problems at the Heliodrom. Five prisoners had attempted suicide. A number of prisoners had been maltreated by members of the 2nd Battalion, 2nd Brigade of the HVO. Fifty prisoners were wounded and six killed in August. Bozic says the ICRC was here and complained in August about conditions at the Heliodrom and about prisoners being taken for labour on the front lines, a practice specifically noted by the ICRC as forbidden by the Geneva Conventions. 186 prisoners had been transferred from Ljubuski to the Heliodrom, and Bozic reminded Coric that he, Coric, was being kept informed about conditions and events at the Heliodrom by his, that is Bozic's, daily reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do apologise to my learned friend. Perhaps at page 58, line 3, there appears to be an error regarding the transcript page. I wonder if that could be clarified. I'm very grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I would be happy to go back and address -- will be happy to go back and check it and if I'm mistaken, Counsel, my apology. I'll just mention in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. Exhibit P 04186, P 04406, and P 05563. And I'll leave the topic of the Heliodrom and go on to Ljubuski. The HVO military police, in fact, had its headquarters in Ljubuski, in the same complex that included the Ljubuski prison, and those having their offices there at the HVO military police administration must have had a daily opportunity to be up close and personal with the -- with the goings and comings and the conduct and events at the Ljubuski prison. Witness E, an HVO military police commander, reported, for example, on the 12th of July, 1993, that 237 Muslims arrested in Rama or Prozor by the HVO military police had been brought to Ljubuski. And that can also be found in Exhibit P 03401, and in transcript pages 22074 to 22076. Among other problems and crimes related to Ljubuski was the fact that HVO soldiers, including soldiers from Tuta's units, often entered the prison and mistreated the prisoners without being stopped, without being prevented from that happening. Witness E again stated that the prison warden at Ljubuski was subordinate to the military police administration. That's at transcript page 22132 to 22133. Witness E testified to receiving orders, both orally and in writing, from both Valentin Coric and Berislav Pusic to transfer prisoners from Ljubuski to the Heliodrom. Witness E -- and that can be found -- excuse me that can be found at transcript pages 22042 to 45 and 22050 to 22053. Witness E also testified that it was a general Practice for the HVO to take prisoners from Ljubuski for forced labour and that Coric was put on notice of this. And that's at transcript page 22013 through 22016. Turning to Dretelj, the 3rd Company of the 5th Battalion military police was in charge of security at Dretelj, and its commander again reported to the military police administration on a daily basis. Valentin Coric himself visited Dretelj shortly after the HVO began bringing Muslims to Dretelj. He had a meeting with a group of officials who were in charge of detention camps in the Capljina area including Gabela and Dretelj. All of this was given in evidence -- includes evidence from Witness C, who confirmed a daily report for the 10th of July, 1993, concerning this meeting, which is also addressed at transcript pages 22417 to 22418. I will also refer the Chamber simply to Exhibits P 0337 and P 03794 as additional exhibits detailing and connecting in various respects Mr. Coric to the Dretelj prison and events there. I'll pause longer on Exhibit P 03630. P 03630 is a report to Coric by Bosko Buntic and Ivica Kraljevic on the 22nd of July, 1993, reporting six deaths at Dretelj, including three persons executed by an HVO military policeman named Vulic. Kasim Kahrimanvic was beaten to death in a solitary cell by an HVO soldier. And there's also reference in the report to the probability that 29 other detainees who could not be accounted for have been thrown into the Neretva River. The report goes on to mention regular physical assaults of prisoners by military policemen at Dretelj with the knowledge of their commanders. Witness C provided additional information about the administration of the camp which can be found at transcript pages 22380 to 22381. Turning very briefly to Gabela again one of the principal HVO prison camps, Heliodrom, Ljubuski, Dretelj, Gabela, and here again Muslims who were caught up in the mass arrest in Herzegovina in July and August 1993, many of them wound up especially coming from Stolac and Capljina to Gabela. At least some of these persons were specifically transferred to other camps or released from Gabela on Valentin Coric's orders. Some of the relevant exhibits in this regard are P 03057, P 03960, P 04756, P 04838, P 05302, P 03630, P 04921, P 06729, and P 10190. All those relate specifically to the military police and Gabela prison or camp. A different aspect of the problem of holding prisoners, which in part perhaps relates back to the statement in the exhibit I referred the Chamber to earlier, we have no documentation for these people, was the problem of keeping detainees for long periods of time without classification and without separating the prisoners of war from civilians. One example of this can be found in Exhibit P 03663, a report by the military police official Zvonko Vidovic on the 23rd of July, 1993, concerning a meeting the previous day, on the 22nd of July, in Ljubuski attended by Valentin Coric and all chiefs of departments of the military police administration. It was agreed at the meeting that: "All those persons who have been detained but against whom criminal proceedings have not been initiated or against whom a criminal report has not been filed are, according to the order of the chief of the military police administration," that is Valentin Coric, "are 'unknown' to our department. This refers solely to the large number of Muslims who have been brought unselectively to the central military remand prison and who have since been forgotten." The report goes on to note that having conducted interviews with more than 2.000 of the detained persons, of those 2.000 persons none of them, none of them, "were interesting from the standpoint of crime." Mr. President, looking at the clock it may be time for a break. I can tell the Chamber that we will certainly finish today but not before the break. Or if you want to go longer, I'll be happy to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, continuing on just a few more items. I want to touch briefly, please, on the topic of forced labour, the killing and wounding of detainees while performing forced labour. Again, the Prosecution submits that the Chamber has heard abundant evidence showing that the HVO engaged in a highly systematic use of prisoners and detainees for forced labour, including often under extremely dangerous conditions, often on the front lines. There are -- there is much evidence in the record, both testimonial and documentary, of prisoners being killed while being on forced labour, that is by fire from the other side, prisoners being killed or injured by their HVO custodians, if you will, being beaten, being mistreated in a number of ways. All of this has been amply, we submit, demonstrated by various evidence in the record. Just a few items for present purposes. Once again, Josip Praljak made reports to senior HVO officials complaining about the taking of Muslim prisoners from the Heliodrom for forced labour and testified that he never received any satisfactory response from either Bruno Stojic, Valentin Coric, or Berislav Pusic. Some of that helped can be found at Exhibit P 04233 and in -- and in the trial transcript at pages 14740 to 14741, 14766 to 14769, 14785 to 14786, 14741. Some of that was already included. I think we have -- I think the Chamber has most of that. 147815 also page. The military expert General Pringle again testified in particular that based on these reports when he was confronted or shown these reports and asked to comment on them from the perspective as a superior commander, General Pringle testified that such reports at the very least would have put a commander on notice that this required serious attention and further inquiry as to what was really going on, and that evidence can be found in the trial transcript at pages 24096 to 24097. I would also mention several other exhibits. P 05812, P 05874, P 06819, P 06552, and P 06202, which generally again go to the -- to the use of detainees, particularly at the Heliodrom, in forced labour. Exhibit P 08428 is a compilation of military police administration reports concerning the mistreatment, death, wounding and escape of prisoners of war at forced labour sites during the period July 1993 to March 1994. In his report dated the 22nd of November, 1993, which has already been mentioned in various context this morning, which is Exhibit P 06805, Radoslav Lavric, in this particular respect, noted the following in item 5 of that document: "It was decreed that prisoners could be used for work (arranging the terrain) with the signature of the commander of the military police battalion or brigade with the mandatory submission of an application and a report after their return. Berislav Pusic was authorised, while Mijo Jelic was the brigade commander." I would also refer the Chamber on this topic to the further testimony of Witness E, which can be found at transcript 22081 to 22083, and Exhibits P 03401, P 04101. Two other particular exhibits are interesting for dual purposes. P 022 -- I have to check this number. I see another -- too many numbers have once again slipped in, Your Honour. I'll have to check this site. Perhaps we can check. 22 -- it must be 02669. And Exhibit P 03345, are reports, and we will get the correct -- we'll verify the correct number of the first exhibit as soon as we can. Both of those documents talk about the movement of prisoners under the control of the military police administration and Mr. Coric. One of them is a request from Mr. Coric to Marijan Biskic, chief of the republic of the Croatian military police administration, talking about the movement of prisoners back and forth between Herceg-Bosna and the republic of Croatia. P 03445, in particular, is a document on -- dated the 10th of July, 1993, where Coric confirmed that a number of prisoners from the Ljubuski prison were being taken to the Lora prison in Split as agreed with the Croatian army military police. Finally on this topic I would also refer the Chamber to P 002541, an HVO order going back to the 27th of May, 1993, transferring a number of prisoners, most of whom had originally been collected if you will from Prozor and Jablanica, and they were being moved on this location from Ljubuski to Heliodrom on the orders of Valentin Coric and Berislav Pusic. Turning next specifically to the deportation of Bosnian Muslims, and we've talked earlier about forcible transfers and expulsions in general, but now specifically on deportation the sense of moving them across the national border to another country. Here again, and at this point based on much of the evidence that was discussed yesterday and much of the evidence that was presented this morning by Mr. Stringer, the evidence shows that the HVO had a again, once again, a systematic structure in place and process in place to move Muslims from Herceg-Bosna out of the country. The Chamber's heard extensive evidence on that. The necessity for getting a letter of guarantee. The necessity of getting a transit visa through Croatia. Groups of refugees and displaced persons, Muslims that showed up in Zagreb thinking they would be taken care of only to be basically abandoned as they got off the bus or the truck in Zagreb with nowhere else to go as one example. Other prisoners and displaced persons being moved to some of the facilities on some of the Croatian islands. The Chamber will recall a great deal of that evidence. Mr. Coric and the military police were right in the middle of all of that. Valentin Coric used his power as chief of HVO military police to unlawfully deport Bosnian Muslims who were imprisoned in HVO camps at Dretelj, Ljubuski, Vitina, and the Heliodrom, and some of the exhibits on that -- supporting that are P 10187 and P 10178. And before I continue, if I can go back and correct the earlier exhibit number. The correct number would be P 02969, the one that I didn't have a moment ago. Returning to deportation, it can be noted generally that Valentin Coric had the power to release prisoners from HVO prisons and detention facilities. I refer you to Exhibit P 02206, which gives an account on the 6th of May, 1993, reporting the implementation of an order by Valentin Coric for the release of 87 prisoners from Ljubuski. Again as just mentioned, as part of the HVO plan Muslims who obtained letters of guarantee from a third country could be released from HVO prisons and camps if they left Herceg-Bosna and travelled by transit visa through Croatia to a third country. As chief of the military police, Coric coordinated this plan with Croatian authorities, reported back to the Herceg-Bosna authorities, and was kept regularly briefed by his subordinates in the HVO military police. All of that is supported in part by Exhibits P 02959, P 04297, P 10187, which I'd mentioned earlier, P 10188, and P 10191. Witness E also discussed this system and Mr. Coric's involvement in it at some length at the trial transcript pages 22033 to 34, actually continuing on to 35, 22087 to 22089, also at 22091 to 22092. Exhibit P 04572 is just an exemplar, if you will, one example of a certificate issued by the 4th Battalion HVO military police on the 27th of August, 1993, stating: "This is to certify that chief Valentin Coric issued an order that all Muslim detainees in possession of guarantee letters and transit visas are released from detention." I would also refer the Chamber to Exhibit -- I think I already have, in fact. P 10187 and again P 10188. Again the interesting thing about those two documents that do merit some additional pause is that they give a record, and the way that they are -- the departure of these Muslims are described is they are being "exiled" from Herzegovina. P 10187, for example, says: "In accordance with the law and pursuant to the order of the chief of military police, Mr. Valentin Coric, we ask the command in Dretelj to release all the people of Muslim ethnicity who possess letters of guarantee. The detainees, including in particular a Zulfikar Jazvin and Samir Jazvin, who were in the military prisons in Dretelj or Gabela, should be handed over to the Ljubuski military police because their families are in Ljubuski and they are being exiled from Herzegovina." A couple of, if the Court will allow me, I might call them miscellaneous items. Going back to the topic of forced labour, I would again refer the Chamber, if I didn't already, to Exhibit P 00740. This is a SIS report dated the 13th of November, 1992, in which Josip Praljak confirms that: "Up until 27 October 1992, the process of taking out prisoners to work involved certification of the request by one of the individuals in charge of logistics and verbal notification of Valentin Coric, chief of the HZ HB military police administration." "According to other information contained in that report, Exhibit P 00740, when complaints were raised about the taking out of prisoners, Valentin Coric issued a decision announcing that no one was allowed to take out prisoners without his signature." I would also mention in closing, just to remind in connection with Mr. Coric and his overall role in the joint criminal enterprise, his senior position in that enterprise, the Chamber will recall the evidence that I discussed yesterday where it was in early April 1993, in connection with the meeting about what we do if Izetbegovic doesn't sign the proposed joint statement, and saying in the meeting involving Boban, Prlic, and others, "We will implement it anyway," giving the deadline of 15 April. In connection with that time period, it was Slobodan Praljak accompanied by Mr. Coric, the two of them together, who were sent as the emissaries, if you will, to Central Bosnia to brief Blaskic, Kordic, and others on the most recent developments and the way forward. Praljak and Coric together. The record again of that meeting again is P 01788. I'll close the submission, Your Honour, concerning Mr. Coric with going back again to the presidential transcript evidence, and I have to give the Chamber some better sense of some of this material prepared that I can show you some visual images of this. This is Exhibit P 06581, a meeting of Tudjman and others with the Herceg-Bosna leadership on the 10th of November, 1993. And I said here pages 20 to 29, but to be more precise for purposes of the record, the excerpts can be found at 20 to 21 and 25 to 29. There is a number of interesting things, Your Honour, in this particular record, one is that -- the discussion you will see in a moment about Valentin Coric. The more general point is this is a meeting which you will see Tudjman, with the Herceg-Bosna leadership around him, hand picks and approves the next Herceg-Bosna leadership. If we go on -- so Granic says, and we're picking up -- but actually it stops. There's even a third relevant component and that is the destruction of the Old Bridge, the Stari Mostar, a few days before this meeting and that's what leads into this part of the conversation. Dr. Mate Granic, whom the Chamber will recall was the Foreign Minister of Croatia: "I have a proposal, the most important things is what the Spanish Battalion will say as the most authoritative. Therefore, my proposal is that someone who is the most trustworthy go immediately, someone who has a connection. Their statement is of the utmost importance. To have that information, to have everything, because if they give good information that that is an exception," that what happened was exceptional, "because otherwise on CNN ..." And then Tudjman comes in and interrupts Granic and says: "Well, between us, the destruction in the military sense, to whose advantage is it? "Mate Boban: Ours." Jukic, the new HVO minister of defence, or the person who's about to become Tudjman's selection, the new Herceg-Bosnian minister of defence. Jukic says: "It's my opinion that we should go for the collapse." In other words, that's our story. "So we'll say it was the destruction or collapse of the bridge, since the rain damaged it and so on. We should make an accusation against war events and the complete destruction of all assets in Bosnia and Herzegovina, so that those who provoked and are continuing the war are the ones who can't, it is impossible to simply approach facilities, and therefore the Assembly in Mostar is being destroyed and so forth. "Jadranko Prlic: It is absolutely beyond our control and that is well known. The line is 300 metres in fronts of it. Therefore there is no way that our men reached the bridge." Well, if the Chamber will recall, there was the strip of ABiH-controlled or Muslim-controlled territory on the right bank between the river and the Bulevar, which was indeed something perhaps like 300 metres, and which apparently is what Mr. Prlic is referring to. "Well, our men couldn't have actually physically got to the bridge," but of course -- then someone comes in and says, "Well, -- but grenades, shells, and so forth." And then Tudjman comes in and says: "All right. Let's go on." Then they go to the topic of selecting the Herceg-Bosna leaders. "Jadranko Prlic: Then it will have to be done ... for education, culture and sports, it was Jozo Maric up until now. He will have to resign from the other appointments that he holds as president of Grude municipality and everything else, and he must absolutely be here. Now, these four state ministries which are the most important ones and where it is the most difficult to find a solution. For the Minister of Finance, I propose Neven Tomic, who is the current Finance Minister. Minister of justice... finance Minister. I suggested Neven Tomic." I guess he's repeating himself. "For the Minister of Justice we propose a change. I want to talk to Slobodan Bozic. He is currently the deputy defence minister and he did not accept. There is Mato Tadic from Posavina, from Brcko. Last night we reached the conclusion," this is Prlic talking "my vice-president, Kresimir Zubak, could perhaps take up the post of Minister of Justice. This is that circle of people. There is no controversy; if these two cannot, then Kresimir Zubak is the minister. Kresimir Zubak is from Usora; he was vice-president in the government up to now. "I too was supposed to remain as vice-president, but as things have turned out now, I haven't been able to find Mate Tadic in Brcko and I cannot appoint someone without talking to him." Then there was some intervention. "For what post? "Well, that is for judiciary and administration. In addition there are two ministers left, the minister of interior and the Ministry of Defence. The president proposed Valentin Coric for the Interior Ministry, the defence minister. On the basis of the discussions we are conducting, I think that a change would be good at the present moment. The president said last night that this question should not be settled without reaching agreement with Mr. Susak. "Of the people down there who can do that, in my view, there is Ante Jelavic, the current logistics commander, by all parameters. And after last night's talk with the president, I had another idea which I think would be rather good. "Valentin Coric, who also enjoys general confidence in the army, is now our commander of the military police. By all his attributes," and this is in November of 1993, Your Honours, and I submit to the Chamber to consider the evidence you have heard today about the conduct and the behaviour of the military police and of the camps and of the prisons and of the deportation and of the expulsions. "By all his attributes, I even think he would be a good defence minister. As for the minister of the interior, that is a matter which needs to be discussed, let us get Mr. Mario Plejic now works here in ... He is from down there. He was born in Mostar and he is from those parts." President Tudjman comes in: "For those two ministries, the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of the Interior, you must appoint the most forceful and most authoritative individuals. "Jadranko Prlic: Valentin is -- Coric absolutely is that, yes. "Mate Boban: I think Valentin as the deputy with Mr. Jarnjak, trained the first Croatian policemen there and since then he has been the commander of the military police. "Tudjman: Good, that is, I think how much is it ... "Mate Boban: But I think he knows the structure of the police especially in war. I think the civilian police should have a defining role in the sense ... "Tudjman: The post of minister of the interior would be a better solution for him if you ..." Someone says: "He is not acquainted with matters. "Jadranko Prlic: It is a good solution except that you always have to -- no one has to take it into account. It is a good solution; he can be both. I even think that he can make a better defence minister. There is always the military, civilian police, one ... I want to say that their chief came from the competition. Then Granic comes back in: "So is it a proposal? "Prlic: I don't know let's see. I think Valentin is ready for both one and the other. "Tudjman: Who is the other candidate for minister of the police and the interior Marijan Plejic. "Mate Boban: He can't. He's here ... He came from Germany. He's a really nice a really nice fellow but he's a quiet person. "President Tudjman: Let me be forthright, gentlemen. I don't know exactly. I don't know all these people. If Perica Jukic is the most forceful person and a person one can count on the most, then I suggest that he be appointed to the position of one of those ministers, either for the interior or for defence, and Coric would be the second and vice Premier. "Jadranko Prlic: Our Perica? "Jukic: Yes. I accept at once, absolutely, without any objections." Tudjman goes on and talks about: "As far as I heard and as much as I can conclude, let us consult each other. Because these two ministers, I think Coric can head one" -- these two ministries, excuse me, "I think Coric can head one, it seems to me he can, regardless and precisely because of that, let him unite them; it can also be, I think the Ministry of the Interior, but be that as it may, those state ministries need cooperation. Maybe I would rather be in favour of -- in view of the problems of the army, such as it is, and as various Rajic's and Bozic's appear and cooperation and so forth, perhaps I would rather be in favour of a vice-Premier for the army, because there is the problem of coordination between the government and that command, which is again complicated and so forth. But also there are personal affinities. "Perico [phoen]: What are you by profession?" This is the person being discussed. Juric -- or Jukic: "I'm an electrical engineer." As I said, Your Honour, several points: The reason that I refer to that transcript at length is number one I think it speaks about the person in the role of Valentin Coric in the joint criminal enterprise, the views about him and the way he was held by his -- the co-members of that enterprise, notwithstanding the evidence that the Prosecution has outlined to you today. Their active endorsement as minister of interior or minister of defence. And I also give the Chamber that evidence as further evidence on the question of Croatia's control over the HVO and the Herceg-Bosna. The Chamber has just looked into the -- behind closed doors that Tudjman and Susak and others selecting the next leadership of Herceg-Bosna. Mr. President, Your Honours, it's the Prosecution case concerning Mr. Coric that as Mr. Stringer said concerning Mr. Pusic, this was a man who played a high and substantial role in the Herceg-Bosna HVO apparatus, a key member and an integral part of the joint criminal enterprise, who played in a very important role and made substantial contributions to the carrying out and implementation of that enterprise. And in that respect, whether it's either on the basis of a joint criminal enterprise form 1 as involving intended crimes or as a joint criminal enterprise form 3 in terms of other crimes which, if not originally intended, either became part of the intended crimes as the JCE evolved or, if not, were nonetheless foreseeable consequences of the carrying out of the conduct, the behaviour, the policy, and the strategy that the Chamber has heard so much evidence about, and therefore, Mr. Coric and the counts against him should remain in the case on each count of the amended indictment. Your Honour, a couple of other items that I must address, I believe. I will just in passing -- the Chamber may recall that at the conclusion of the submissions made by the Coric Defence the issue of cumulative charging was raised. I think with all -- with all due respect that can be handled quite quickly. Cumulative charging is a well-established and accepted form of pleading at the Tribunal. It has been for many years. There should be no confusion or misunderstanding that there is a difference between cumulative charging, which is absolutely acceptable, and cumulative or multiple convictions for the same behaviour and sentencing. Those matters are to be sorted out in the judgement and in sentencing if the Chamber, of course, gets to that point, and then we'll sort out which counts or which basis, if it's going to be an article 5 charge, crime against humanity, or a grave breach charge or something, which charge the Chamber may ultimately pick as the appropriate charge for purposes of conviction and sentencing. That is by no means a facet or aspect that should be dealt with in the context of 98 bis. It is premature at most or at best to consider any such arguments. Finally, Your Honours, I turn back to what the Prosecution considers may be the surviving aspects, if I can put it that way, or remaining aspects of the Petkovic submissions on several legal points which the Chamber may recall from last week, which again I can make brief response to. The Prosecution position on those points, and that deals with the issue of co-perpetration, indirect perpetration, the pleading of one aspect of the joint criminal enterprise. Those are the issues, and these were in fact addressed in the Prosecution's written submissions filed on the 7th of March, 2007, but let me just take two minutes to emphasise or summarise the basic three points of the Prosecution response to the Petkovic arguments. First, the Prosecution does not agree that certain paragraphs or parts of paragraphs need to be stricken from the indictment. As we said in March 2007, in paragraph 25: "The trial can proceed on the basis that the Trial Chamber will apply the permissible modes of liability under Tribunal jurisprudence." And that remains as true today as it was in March 2007. Of course as to every aspect of the case, the Chamber will ultimately apply the law that it views as the correct and applicable law. This is no different. The Prosecution submits that there's no reason for the Chamber to deal further -- make any specific further rulings on that matter at this time. Going on to the issue or argument about co-perpetration. It may be a linguistic misunderstanding, Your Honour. It is correct, and as the Prosecution again said in the March -- in March of 2007, the Stakic Appeals Chamber did strike down, if you will, or knock out, however one might put it, a particular form of co-perpetration, a particular form, and if the Chamber and the Judges, if you followed the -- some of these developments over the last few years, the Tribunal certainly has looked at various possible theories of co-perpetration. Judge Schomburg has had some theories and that's what happened in the Stakic case. There's been the evolving jurisprudence of joint criminal enterprise, and it is true in the Stakic appeal one particular form of co-perpetration was stricken, but that is not the form of co-perpetration charged in the indictment. We do not understand the Defence, in particular the Petkovic Defence, to be arguing that there is no form of co-perpetration at the Tribunal. Every legal system, I submit, has some forms of co-perpetration; that is, how two or more persons commit crimes together, and I'm sure no one is suggesting that there is no mode of liability at the Tribunal at which two or more persons can be held responsible for commission of a crime. So indeed co-perpetration continues to exist. The particular form of co-perpetration charged in this case is joint criminal enterprise in its various forms. The same can be said about indirect perpetration. Again I think that if anything, there may be some misunderstanding. I dare say that if -- in most if not all legal systems there is again the concept that one can commit crimes through and by way of other persons even as innocent actors who do not themselves have necessarily the requisite mens rea but are simply a tool or an instrument used by others to commit a crime. That is indirect perpetration. I don't commit the physical act, the actus reus of the crime, but I cause or obtain its commission by someone else. Again, I don't think anyone would say that there is no such form of perpetration at the Tribunal. I suspect that neither Milosevic nor Krajisnik nor Brdjanin nor any of the other leaders physically carried out any of the crimes on the ground but indeed acted through other persons. So that is the basic submission on that point, Your Honour. There is indirect perpetration, just as there is co-perpetration. The final issue on this is the language used in paragraph 226 of the amended indictment which says, and I don't have it right in front of me at the moment, but says something to the effect or can be interpreted as saying -- suggesting aiding and abetting a joint criminal enterprise. And as the Prosecution conceded in March 2007, it is correct that there is no form of liability called aiding and abetting a joint criminal enterprise. However, the Chamber does look at the language in paragraph 226, we again submit that the Chamber can apply the proper and applicable law and that nothing in that paragraph needs to be stricken or amended in any way in order for the Chamber to apply the appropriate law. At most, at most, the Chamber might consider striking the language about four or five words that -- the portion that says "those systems (or either of them)," to the extent that that might be interpreted as suggesting aiding and abetting a joint criminal enterprise, but that very same language goes on to say "aiding and abetting persons in those matters," and that is certainly clearly a standard statement of aiding and abetting law. "One aids and abets persons in the commission of crime," a person being aided and abetted typically being referred to as the principal, "a person," and paragraph 226 clearly states and can be and should be read as stating in that relevant part "for substantially aiding and abetting persons who participated in them." And the Prosecution respectfully submits there's nothing objectionable or improper about that language. Your Honour, with that, I think the Prosecution has addressed what it considers the outstanding questions and the submissions made by the various Defence teams, and we thank the Chamber, Mr. President, and all of Your Honours, for your attention to our submissions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much, Mr. Scott. So you have ended the submissions with respect to Rule 98 bis with regard to the Prosecution. As you know, the Chamber will hand down an oral decision. You will be informed of the date of that hearing. We are going to make sure that it be handed down as soon as possible. So a Scheduling Order will be given to you, and we will get together or we will reconvene for the reading of this decision. Everything was said. Thank you very much, and this hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened sine die
